title: How to Make Marble Clay Diyas for Diwali, Step by Step
excerpt: White clay, bright colours rolled to a marbled 1/4 inch, a pinched tip, 45 minutes in the oven and gold rims — a Diwali craft children can actually do.
body:
• Marble clay diyas are made by rolling white clay, adding cubes of coloured clay, and re-rolling to a 1/4-inch thickness so the colours swirl instead of mixing flat.
  • Cut a round, shape it into a small bowl, pinch one tip to a point, then bake at 265 degrees F for 45 minutes, per HGTV's guide by Nisha Vedi Pawar.
  • Finish with gold paint on the rims and use a tea light instead of oil and a wick for a mess-free, child-friendly lamp.
  • Start this weekend: the HGTV version needs oven time plus cooling, and air-dry alternatives need several hours to overnight to harden before painting.

A diya is a small clay oil lamp lit at Diwali to symbolize knowledge, power and wealth, and the triumph of light over darkness. The marble version replaces a single painted colour with swirls of many: white clay rolled out as a base, bright clay worked through it, and a gold-painted rim once the lamp is baked. HGTV's guide, created by Nisha Vedi Pawar, is designed as a kids' craft, and it swaps the traditional oil and wick for a tea light — easier and mess-free for a family table.

How the marbling works

Line a baking tray with parchment paper and roll out the white clay. Set cubes of coloured clay on top, then roll the layers together and keep working the clay with your hands until it reaches a 1/4-inch thickness. How you combine the colours changes the pattern: stacking colours before rolling gives a different swirl from folding them in, so one batch can produce a set of diyas that match without being identical.

Shaping and baking

Cut a round from the rolled clay with a cookie cutter or a small bowl, shape the disc into a small bowl, and pinch one tip of the bowl into the pointed end of a traditional diya. Repeat with the remaining clay, arrange the diyas on the tray, and bake in a preheated oven at 265 degrees F for 45 minutes. Let them cool to room temperature before painting the rims gold; once the paint is dry, set a tea light in each one.

The air-dry alternative

If you would rather skip the oven, NurtureStore's clay diya guide uses air-dry clay and a pinch-pot method: knead a handful of clay, roll it into a ball, push a thumb into the centre and pinch outward until the holder fits a tea light, then push down one part of the wall to form a lip. Air-dry diyas need several hours, or overnight, to harden before acrylic paint, biodegradable glitter or sequins go on. NurtureStore links the lamp to the story of Rama and Sita, whose homecoming the lights are said to guide — a useful story to tell children while the clay dries.

For diaspora families

Polymer and air-dry clay, tea lights and gold acrylic paint are standard stock in US craft stores, so the project needs no specialty shopping. Make the diyas a day ahead of your Diwali gathering so baking, cooling and painting are not competing with cooking, and keep lit tea lights on a heat-safe surface and attended, as with any flame.

steps.detail: Line a baking tray with parchment paper; roll white clay out as the base layer with a rolling pin.
Place cubes of coloured clay on the white, roll together and work by hand to a 1/4-inch thickness; stacking colours before rolling changes the swirl.
Cut a round with a cookie cutter or small bowl, shape it into a small bowl, and pinch one tip to a point.
Bake on the tray in a preheated oven at 265 degrees F for 45 minutes.
Cool to room temperature, paint the rims gold, and let the paint dry.
Set a tea light in each finished diya instead of oil and a wick for a mess-free lamp.
